messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
John, a 28-year-old European American male, is a social media manager who has recently returned from military service. In his late teens and early twenties, John had always felt a strong sense of duty and wanted to serve his country. However, the reality of his deployment proved far more challenging than he anticipated. During one particularly harrowing mission in Afghanistan, John witnessed several comrades sustain severe injuries while under enemy fire. The scene was chaotic, with explosions, gunfire, and the cries of wounded soldiers filling the air. One of his closest friends suffered a devastating leg injury, and the sight of him being evacuated on a stretcher has stayed with John ever since. Since returning home, John’s life has been marked by an array of unsettling triggers and maladaptive strategies. He finds himself hypervigilant when he encounters visible injuries or wounds on others, which often happens in his role as a social media manager where he frequently interacts with posts about current events and human suffering. The sound of helicopters or aircraft can quickly plunge him into a state of high anxiety, reminiscent of the missions flown over rugged terrain. Driving with other people has become a source of significant distress for John, as it often reminds him of those tense moments on patrol when any vehicle could be a potential threat. This has led to his decision to avoid driving with others whenever possible, which has strained his relationship with his partner and colleagues who rely on him for carpooling. John’s avoidance behaviors extend to military uniforms or weapons, which he now actively steers clear of. Even the sight of a police officer in uniform can trigger intense discomfort. He frequently rehearses what he will say before any social interaction, afraid that unexpected questions might expose his vulnerabilities. Additionally, he has begun to avoid situations that put physical stress on his body, such as exercise or even minor exertions like carrying groceries. At night, John struggles with sleep due to a constant need for vigilance, believing that staying alert is crucial for his safety. When triggered by auditory cues or visual reminders of the trauma, he experiences strong physical reactions, such as increased heart rate and sweating. Unexpected touches often startle him severely, making him jump in alarm. John's memory of the traumatic event is fragmented and disjointed; it comes to him in disconnected pieces that don’t fit together coherently. Sometimes, he feels the full emotional intensity of the experience without any clear image or memory to anchor these feelings. The extreme nature of what he witnessed makes it difficult for him to believe that this actually happened to him, as if it is something out of a movie. John’s negative appraisals have taken root deeply within him. He feels like an outsider now, unable to fully connect with people who haven’t shared his experiences. He often thinks that someone else would not have gotten into the situation he was in, wondering why he couldn't have handled it differently or avoided it altogether. The belief that he has permanently changed for the worse adds a layer of despair and isolation. These symptoms have gradually eroded John’s sense of self and relationships. His partner has grown increasingly concerned about his withdrawal and anxiety, leading to several heated arguments and a deepening rift in their relationship. At work, his avoidance behaviors and hypervigilance have made it difficult for him to collaborate effectively with colleagues, causing tension and affecting his job performance. Ultimately, the cumulative strain of these symptoms and the impact on his personal life finally drove John to seek help. He is now most afraid that he will never fully recover from what happened, but at the same time, he hopes that therapy can provide him with tools to manage his anxiety and rebuild his connections with others.
